claim: Dung-style semantics are fully determined by the attack graph; the grounded extension is unique and computable by iteration in polynomial time, so code can run S7 survival cheaply.
agent_test: Run grounded on candidate graphs; check runtime and agreement with a brute-force check.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Naive instantiation of structured arguments can violate rationality postulates (two contradictory conclusions accepted); an attack-type and preference layer (ASPIC+) is needed, and it is a source of error.
agent_test: Count contradictory-survivor cases in our graphs with and without preference handling.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-10 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Humans judging 12 small AFs match grounded about 75% and CF2 about 75% (chance 33%); preferred 68%. BUT later and earlier studies by the same group show grounded is the worst predictor on floating reinstatement (0% to 2.5% in science and maths sets) and on a 3-cycle (12% vs CF2 56%). All human data come from one Luxembourg lab and student samples.
agent_test: Compare our code's survivor set to human or judge labels on small graphs; report match by semantics.

claim: Among 49 coherent participants 22 follow a grounded-like skeptical strategy and 27 do not; most of the 27 fit CF2 in 11 of 12 AFs (not the six-cycle: CF2 33%, preferred and semi-stable 60%). Grounded is the safe default but not what most people do when candidates tie.
agent_test: Use grounded as default; test CF2-like cycle handling on cyclic graphs only.

claim: Simple reinstatement cannot separate semantics; floating reinstatement and cycles do. Rahwan et al. 2010 (abstract only) and the Luxembourg studies agree that people do not behave like grounded there; a 2024 experiment replicates that reinstated arguments are rated lower than unattacked ones.
agent_test: Check how often our candidate graphs contain odd cycles or floating cases; if rare, the semantics choice is moot.

claim: A new semantics (SCF2) fits the 61-person data slightly better than CF2 and grounded but not significantly; evidence for it is weak.
agent_test: Not worth testing before basic grounded S7.

claim: Frozen LLMs are poor at computing even the grounded extension zero-shot: 0.15 (GPT-3.5) to 0.54 (GPT-4o) on AFs of 6 to 25 arguments. Code must compute survivors, not the model.
agent_test: Give the model an AF in text, compare its survivor list with code at equal tokens.

claim: Supervised fine-tuning raises grounded accuracy to 0.95 to 0.97 and conflict-free output to 1.00, but fine-tuning is outside our no-training constraint.
agent_test: Not applicable; use as an upper bound for the code route.

claim: Training with explanations generalises better to larger AFs (0.85/0.78 grounded/complete vs 0.68/0.56 without, Qwen); without explanation accuracy fell to about 30%.
agent_test: Test whether step-by-step trace prompts help a frozen model on larger graphs.

claim: Graph neural networks learn semantics almost perfectly (MCC 0.997 to 1.0) on AFs up to 25 arguments, but exact solvers remain the reference and complete-semantics recall needs a verifier (0.41 to 0.91).
agent_test: Use exact solvers in code; no need for learned solvers at our graph sizes.

claim: In ArgLLM claim verification (bipolar tree, DF-QuAD), neutral 0.5 base scores trail CoT by about 0.03 to 0.17; LLM-estimated base scores come within about 0.03 in most cells (not all, e.g. Gemma 2 9B 0.53 vs 0.61).
agent_test: At equal tokens compare CoT vs argument-tree scoring with estimated base scores on 2 datasets.

claim: Deeper argument trees (depth 2, 7 nodes) do not reliably beat depth 1 (3 nodes); differences go both ways.
agent_test: Vary tree depth at equal token budget; expect flat.

claim: With a strong model (GPT-4o) on MedClaim all methods sit at 0.51 to 0.58, and ArgLLM variants (0.51 to 0.53) are below CoT (0.58): the scaffold gives no gain where base ability is the limit.
agent_test: Check on a hard item set whether graph scoring helps when all candidates are weak.

claim: Direct prompting beats argumentative confidence estimates in many UQ comparisons (up to 0.130 accuracy higher; 44 of 74 significant intervals favour it); LUQ was best 10 times. Graph scoring is not a free calibration win.
agent_test: Compare confidence from graph score vs direct prompt on Brier score at equal tokens.

claim: Combining argument graphs with retrieval raises claim accuracy (PubHealth GPT-4.1-mini 0.898 vs 0.838 no retriever; plain RAG fell to 0.647-0.670; RAGuard GPT-3.5 0.804 vs 0.768), but gains shrink for strong models (GPT-4o-mini 0.855 vs 0.840).
agent_test: Test graph filtering of retrieved notes vs plain concatenation.

claim: Multi-LLM argument meshing (MArgE) beats debate by up to 8.4 points and loses at most 2.6; with a stronger scorer gains reach about 20 points, but it beats CoT by only 1.0 to 3.5 points on two of three datasets.
agent_test: Mesh candidates from several samples of one model and score by code; compare with majority vote.

claim: Argumentation-based multi-agent forecasting lifted Metaculus accuracy from 68% to 81% and GJOpen 63% to 75% in best variants; gains were smaller where the agent was already strong.
agent_test: Low priority; domain is forecasting.

claim: LLMs extract attack and support relations imperfectly: best open model macro F1 75 (RoBERTa baseline about 68); attack F1 trails support F1. The edge-building step is the weak point of S7.
agent_test: Measure our edge judge against hand labels on 50 candidate pairs.

claim: LLM judging of non-linear debates is weak without structure (Spearman about 0.11 vanilla vs 0.46 CoT few-shot on DebatePedia), and graph order in the prompt changes results (MCC +8.14 GPT-4o, -16.48 Claude-3.5-sonnet).
agent_test: Shuffle candidate order in S7 prompts and report variance.

claim: Graph cycles matter: pairwise protocols produce cyclicity 0 where grounded and preferred coincide; cross-pair arbitration yields 0.20 to 0.29 cyclic share. Semantics choice matters only once cycles appear.
agent_test: Log cyclic share in our candidate graphs.

claim: Formal argumentation in multi-agent requirements negotiation raised compliance coverage to 84.7% vs 47.6-47.8% for baselines, but trace completeness is only 40.9%.
agent_test: Out of domain; note only.

claim: Untuned LLM base scores rank arguments poorly (Spearman about 0.525); trained combinations reach TFU 0.668-0.677 vs direct SFT 0.659 (garbled table, direction only).
agent_test: Do not rely on these numbers.

claim: Argument-graph features predict persuasion barely above chance (AUC about 0.56; logistic regression 0.587; n=384).
agent_test: Do not use graph shape alone as a quality signal.

claim: Case-based argumentative reasoning with LLMs (AAM-CBR) beats single prompts on synthetic data at 10 factors (1.00/0.96 vs 0.90) but collapsed at 6 factors for a small model (0.28 vs 0.76).
agent_test: Check whether structured reasoning fails on small inputs; synthetic data.

claim: Base scores matter: in ARGORA LLM-assigned scores beat constant 0.5 (MMLU-Pro 0.638 vs 0.618; GPQA 0.523 vs 0.419) but nobody measured their calibration (no Brier or ECE); Baba and Chudziak state base scores and edge polarities are never checked.
agent_test: Ablation: uniform 0.5 vs LLM-estimated base scores; measure accuracy.

claim: Position of candidates changes LLM judge verdicts: pairwise consistency 0.57 to 0.82 for most judges, list-wise 0.34 to 0.68, worse when candidates are close in quality. No study measured this for attack-edge labels between candidate answers.
agent_test: Judge each edge in both orders; keep only edges that agree; measure survivor-set change.

claim: Majority voting over samples matches or beats natural-language debate at equal agent count (Qwen2.5-7B average 0.7691 vs best debate 0.7377, single 0.7205). The baseline an attack-graph survival rule must beat is voting, not CoT.
agent_test: Always run a vote baseline at the same token count.

claim: In the one compute-matched argumentation test found (3 experts vs MV3), the argument graph gave small gains: MMLU-Pro 0.638 vs 0.618, MedQA equal at 0.812, with significant paired reversal tests on 3 of 7 sets. It used trees and DF-QuAD, not Dung grounded.
agent_test: Replicate with Dung grounded on cyclic candidate graphs.

claim: Large gains over CoT are reported when a verifier agent actively attacks each decision (ArgMed-Agents GPT-4 MedQA 71.4 to 83.3, n=300) but at several times the token cost and with no vote baseline; another group has not replicated it.
agent_test: Cost-matched comparison of verifier-attack loop vs vote.

claim: Human attack-edge judgments between short natural-language arguments are about 80% correct for well-designed items (74 to 89%), but only 17% to 44% of intended one-way attacks are seen as one-way; item wording changes accuracy from 56% to 84%.
agent_test: Have the edge judge label direction; test on items with known one-way attacks.

claim: People use graded beliefs (4 to 6 values over a dialogue) and rarely accept or reject fully; the 3-state output of Dung semantics oversimplifies. Non-student sample (AMT, 69 people) from a second group.
agent_test: Keep a numeric score with the survive flag.

claim: Random attack graphs among 4 to 6 candidates show cycles in 25% to 56% of graphs at edge density 0.2 and empty grounded sets in 5.6% to 9.1%; at density 0.3 cycles reach 48% to 85%. Real LLM-judged graphs were not measured by any study; this is a simulation only.
agent_test: Log cycle rate and empty-grounded rate in our own S7 runs.

claim: LLM review of argument graphs for structure is flaky (objects to 9.8% of correct graphs, 6.2% verdict change on identical input, 2,758 ms) while code validators are exact and take 1 ms; cycle detection should be code.
agent_test: Code the cycle and dangling-edge checks; do not ask the LLM.

claim: No attack-graph or formal-argumentation study on open-ended or creative tasks was found; nearest evidence says convergence-driven debate cuts diversity (Creative-MAD restores 24% to 26% diversity on Qwen3-8B).
agent_test: On NoveltyBench-like tasks use survival only to drop candidates that fail an objective test.

claim: No measured cost-benefit of ASPIC+-style structured arguments (undercut, preference) versus plain attack edges for LLM agents was found; only theory on rationality postulates (K02) and one schema-field error rate: 21% of graphs had an invalid undeclared scheme field.
agent_test: A/B plain attacks vs attacks+undercut with an error audit.

claim: LLM argument-mining benchmarks show relation identification is unreliable: ArgBench mining scores about 0.31 to 0.60 across 11 LLMs; fine-tuning raises it. Edge labels need verification before survival is computed.
agent_test: Measure edge precision on a hand-labelled sample of our own candidate pairs.
